questions.successCriteria: Student can recall the author, genre, and first performance date of Romeo and Juliet.

questions.stem: Who wrote Romeo and Juliet and when was it first performed?

options.label: A
options.text: William Shakespeare, 1597
options.feedbackCorrect: Correct! Shakespeare wrote this tragedy early in his career, and it was first performed in 1597.

options.label: B
options.text: Christopher Marlowe, 1595
options.feedbackWrong: Not quite. The author is William Shakespeare; Marlowe was a different playwright of the same period.

options.label: C
options.text: William Shakespeare, 1601
options.feedbackWrong: Shakespeare wrote it earlier – the first performance was in 1597, not 1601.

options.label: D
options.text: Ben Jonson, 1597
options.feedbackWrong: Ben Jonson wrote other plays, but Romeo and Juliet is definitely by William Shakespeare.

questions.successCriteria: Student correctly identifies the central feud as the Capulet-Montague family conflict.
questions.ossdExpectation: Read and demonstrate understanding of a variety of texts for different purposes.
questions.alignmentNote: Asking about core conflict checks basic comprehension of the play's framework.
questions.stemIntent: Check if student understands what drives the story's conflict.
questions.commonMisconception: Students may think the conflict is between individual characters (e.g., Romeo vs. Tybalt) rather than families.
questions.stem: What is the central conflict in Romeo and Juliet?

options.label: A
options.text: A war between the cities of Verona and Mantua
options.feedbackWrong: The play is not about a war between cities; it's about a personal feud inside Verona.

options.label: B
options.text: A long-standing feud between the Capulet and Montague families
options.feedbackCorrect: Yes! The entire story is built on the hatred between the two noble families.

options.label: C
options.text: Romeo's argument with his father about marriage
options.feedbackWrong: Romeo's father is not a major source of conflict; the family feud is the driving force.

options.label: D
options.text: A rivalry between two schools in Verona
options.feedbackWrong: There are no schools involved; it's a deadly family rivalry.

questions.successCriteria: Student can identify a major plot event from a list of possibilities.
questions.ossdExpectation: Read and demonstrate understanding of a variety of texts for different purposes.
questions.alignmentNote: This question tests whether the student followed the sequence of events in the tragedy.
questions.stemIntent: Check if student knows the key turning point in the plot.
questions.commonMisconception: Students often forget the order of deaths or the exile, confusing it with other events.
questions.stem: Which of the following is a key event from the plot of Romeo and Juliet?

options.label: A
options.text: Romeo and Juliet hold a public wedding ceremony
options.feedbackWrong: They actually marry in secret, not in public.

options.label: B
options.text: Mercutio is killed by Tybalt, which leads to Romeo's exile
options.feedbackCorrect: Right! Mercutio's death is the turning point that sets Romeo's banishment in motion.

options.label: C
options.text: Juliet's plan to fake her death succeeds without any problems
options.feedbackWrong: The plan goes wrong because Romeo does not receive the message that she is only asleep.

options.label: D
options.text: Romeo kills Prince Escalus in a fight
options.feedbackWrong: Romeo kills Tybalt, not the Prince. Prince Escalus is the ruler of Verona.

questions.successCriteria: Student can go beyond the love story and explain the destructive cost of inter-group hatred as the central theme.
questions.ossdExpectation: Read and demonstrate understanding of a variety of texts for different purposes.
questions.alignmentNote: Asking about theme moves from comprehension to interpretation, fulfilling the 'demonstrate understanding' portion of B1.
questions.stemIntent: Check if student can articulate the lesson's deeper message about hatred.
questions.commonMisconception: Students often reduce the play to a teenage romance and miss the broader social commentary.
questions.stem: According to the lesson, what is the main theme of Romeo and Juliet?

options.label: A
options.text: Young love always overcomes every obstacle
options.feedbackWrong: The play actually shows how love is destroyed by hatred, not how it conquers all.

options.label: B
options.text: Meaningless inter-group hatred can lead to irreversible tragedy
options.feedbackCorrect: Exactly! The lesson emphasized that Shakespeare uses the lovers' deaths to show the terrible cost of the family feud.

options.label: C
options.text: If you believe in fate, everything will end happily
options.feedbackWrong: Fate does not bring happiness here – the 'star-crossed' lovers die.

options.label: D
options.text: Friendship is more important than romantic love
options.feedbackWrong: While friendship is present (Mercutio, Nurse), the central theme is about hatred and its consequences.

questions.successCriteria: Student can match the definition of dramatic irony to an example.
questions.ossdExpectation: Read and demonstrate understanding of a variety of texts for different purposes.
questions.alignmentNote: Identifying literary devices is part of demonstrating understanding of texts under B1.
questions.stemIntent: Check if student knows what dramatic irony means in a dramatic context.
questions.commonMisconception: Students often confuse soliloquy, aside, and dramatic irony because they all involve audience knowledge.
questions.stem: Which of the following is an example of dramatic irony?

options.label: A
options.text: Romeo speaks about his feelings while alone on stage
options.feedbackWrong: That is a soliloquy – a character thinking aloud when alone.

options.label: B
options.text: The audience knows Juliet is just asleep, but Romeo believes she is dead
options.feedbackCorrect: Correct! Dramatic irony occurs when the audience knows something important that a character does not.

options.label: C
options.text: The Nurse makes a joke after a serious scene
options.feedbackWrong: That is comic relief – a humorous moment to lighten the mood.

options.label: D
options.text: Friar Laurence delivers a speech about the power of plants
options.feedbackWrong: That is a monologue – a long speech by one character to others on stage.

reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: The student may think Romeo and Juliet was written by another Elizabethan playwright (e.g., Christopher Marlowe or Ben Jonson) or first performed in a later year (e.g., 1601).

miniLesson.explain: Romeo and Juliet is a tragedy written by William Shakespeare early in his career. It was first performed in 1597 and is set in Verona, Italy, in the 1590s. Knowing this background helps you connect the play to Shakespeare's time and setting.
miniLesson.example: In the lesson, the play was introduced as 'Romeo and Juliet, a tragedy by William Shakespeare, first performed in 1597.' Shakespeare's plays often used Italian settings and themes of family conflict.
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Shakespeare + 1597 + Verona: The Bard's tragic 1590s Italian love story.

guidedPractice.prompt: Fill in the blanks: ______ wrote Romeo and Juliet, and it was first performed in ______.
True or False? Explain your answer: 'Romeo and Juliet was first performed in 1597 and takes place in Verona, Italy.'
guidedPractice.answer: True. The play is a tragedy by William Shakespeare, first performed in 1597, and set in Verona, Italy.

guidedPractice.prompt: In a short paragraph, describe the background of Romeo and Juliet (author, first performance, setting, genre) and explain why this information is useful for understanding the play.
guidedPractice.answer: Romeo and Juliet is a tragedy written by William Shakespeare early in his career. It was first performed in 1597 and is set in 1590s Verona, Italy. Knowing this helps us picture the world of the play and see how the family feud drives the tragedy.

reteachModules.trigger: Student picks wrong option on Q2
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: The student may think the central conflict is something other than the feud between the Capulet and Montague families, such as a war between cities, a personal argument, or a rivalry not involving entire households, and may not realize the feud is long-standing, origin unknown, and extends to servants.

miniLesson.explain: In Romeo and Juliet, the main conflict is not just a quarrel between two individuals. It is a deep-rooted feud between the Capulet and Montague families in Verona, Italy. The origin of this feud is unknown, but it is so strong that it even extends to the servants of both households. This family hatred drives the whole plot: it forces Romeo and Juliet to marry in secret, causes street brawls, leads to Mercutio's death, gets Romeo exiled, and ultimately ends in a failed fake death plan and a double suicide. The lesson emphasizes that this inter-group hatred has a destructive cost, which is the core theme.
miniLesson.example: When Tybalt, a Capulet, kills Mercutio, who is a friend of Romeo, the fight happens because of the family feud. Even though Romeo has just secretly married Juliet, a Capulet, he cannot escape the hatred between the families. That single act of violence leads to Romeo being exiled, which sets the tragedy in motion. The feud makes the lovers' world impossible, and it shows how the conflict affects everyone, from the noble families down to their servants.
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Picture two rival houses with a high wall between them: Capulet on one side, Montague on the other. Even the servants on each side are trapped behind that wall. That wall is the feud, and it makes every attempt to reach across it end in tragedy.

guidedPractice.prompt: Which two families are at war in Romeo and Juliet?
Why is the feud between the Capulets and Montagues considered the central conflict of the play? Give one way it affects the plot.
guidedPractice.answer: The feud is the central conflict because it drives the whole story. For example, it causes street brawls and leads to Mercutio's death, Romeo's exile, and the final double suicide.

guidedPractice.prompt: The feud extends to the servants of both families. If a Capulet servant meets a Montague servant in the street, what might happen based on this fact? How does this connect to the play's core theme?
guidedPractice.answer: They would likely fight or be hostile to each other, even though they are just servants, because the hatred is so deep. This shows that the conflict affects everyone, not just the main characters. It connects to the theme that meaningless inter-group hatred can lead to irreversible tragedy.

reteachModules.trigger: Student selects a wrong answer when asked to identify a key event from the plot of Romeo and Juliet.
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: The student recalls pieces of the story but not the order or cause-and-effect links between them, especially how street brawls, Mercutio's death, Romeo's exile, the failed fake death plan, and the double suicide connect.

miniLesson.explain: Romeo and Juliet are star-crossed lovers from two feuding families. They marry in secret. Street brawls break out, leading to Mercutio's death and Romeo's exile. Later, a fake death plan fails, and the play ends in the double suicide of Romeo and Juliet. The plot moves from love to violence to tragedy because of the hatred between the Capulet and Montague families.
miniLesson.example: Think about the chain: Romeo and Juliet secretly marry → street brawls lead to Mercutio's death → Romeo is exiled → the fake death plan fails → Romeo and Juliet both die. Each event causes the next one.
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Secret marriage → Street brawl → Mercutio dies → Romeo exiled → Fake death fails → Double suicide.

guidedPractice.prompt: Which of these events happens FIRST in Romeo and Juliet: Romeo's exile, double suicide, secret marriage, or Mercutio's death?
guidedPractice.answer: The secret marriage happens first. After Romeo and Juliet marry in secret, the street brawls start, leading to Mercutio's death and Romeo's exile.

guidedPractice.prompt: Put these plot events in the correct order: Romeo's exile, Mercutio's death, double suicide, failed fake death plan.
guidedPractice.answer: Mercutio's death → Romeo's exile → failed fake death plan → double suicide.

guidedPractice.prompt: Summarize the main plot of Romeo and Juliet in 2–3 sentences, making sure to include the secret marriage, Mercutio's death, Romeo's exile, the failed fake death plan, and the double suicide.
guidedPractice.answer: Romeo and Juliet, from feuding families, marry in secret. Street brawls lead to Mercutio's death and Romeo's exile. A failed fake death plan ends in the double suicide of Romeo and Juliet.

reteachModules.trigger: Student picks the wrong option on Q4 (theme interpretation).
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: The student sees Romeo and Juliet mainly as a teenage love story and overlooks the play's central message about the destructive consequences of inter-group hatred.

miniLesson.explain: In Romeo and Juliet, the most important theme is the irreversible destructive cost of meaningless inter-group hatred. Though Romeo and Juliet fall in love, their families—the Capulets and Montagues—are locked in a deep feud. That hatred leads to street brawls, Mercutio's death, Romeo's exile, a failed fake-death plan, and finally the double suicide of the lovers. Shakespeare is not saying love conquers all; he is showing that hatred destroys young love and causes tragedy.
miniLesson.example: Chenpin shared that the story conveys inter-group hatred destroys young love and impulsive decisions lead to danger. For example, the audience knows Juliet is only asleep, but Romeo doesn't—the feud and missed message cause both to die. The lesson's core fact is the theme: reflection on the irreversible destructive cost of meaningless inter-group hatred, not just a teenage love story.
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Hatred is the villain. Whenever you think about Romeo and Juliet, remember: the enemy isn't love—it's the family feud that kills the lovers.

guidedPractice.prompt: In Romeo and Juliet, what destroys Romeo and Juliet's love and leads to the tragedy? (Choose: 'the family feud between the Capulets and Montagues' or 'a disagreement with the Prince'.) Answer in one sentence.
guidedPractice.answer: The family feud between the Capulets and Montagues destroys their love and leads to the tragedy.

guidedPractice.prompt: Explain how the hatred between the Capulet and Montague families causes at least three tragic events from the plot. Use three details from the lesson.
guidedPractice.answer: The hatred causes street brawls, Mercutio's death, Romeo's exile, a failed fake death plan, and the double suicide of Romeo and Juliet. For example: Mercutio is killed, Romeo is sent away, and Juliet's plan to fake her death fails because Romeo doesn't know the truth, so both die.

guidedPractice.prompt: Why is the theme of Romeo and Juliet best described as 'irreversible destructive cost of meaningless inter-group hatred' instead of 'young love conquers all'? Support your answer with facts from the lesson.
guidedPractice.answer: The theme is the destructive cost of inter-group hatred because the Capulet-Montague feud leads directly to Mercutio's death, Romeo's exile, the failed fake-death plan, and the lovers' double suicide. The play's ending shows that the hatred is meaningless and cannot be reversed, while young love does not conquer all—it is destroyed by the feud. Chenpin's example also says inter-group hatred destroys young love and impulsive decisions lead to danger.

reteachModules.trigger: Student selected an incorrect answer on Q5 about dramatic irony.
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: The student may confuse soliloquy, aside, and dramatic irony because they all involve audience knowledge, or mix up the definitions of monologue, comic relief, and other terms.

miniLesson.explain: In Romeo and Juliet, Shakespeare uses five key dramatic terms. A monologue is a long speech by one character to others on stage. A soliloquy is a speech by a character alone on stage, revealing inner thoughts. An aside is a short remark heard only by the audience, not by other characters. Comic relief is a humorous moment that lightens a serious scene. Dramatic irony occurs when the audience knows something important that a character does not.
miniLesson.example: In Act 5, the audience knows Juliet is only asleep, but Romeo believes she is dead—this is dramatic irony. Romeo speaking alone about his feelings is a soliloquy. Friar Laurence's long speech about plants is a monologue. The Nurse's jokes after the fight provide comic relief.
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Remember: Soliloquy = Solo speech; Aside = Audience only; Dramatic irony = Drama in the know; Comic relief = Comedy; Monologue = Many listeners.

guidedPractice.prompt: Which term means the audience knows more than a character? (A) monologue, (B) aside, (C) dramatic irony, (D) comic relief
In Romeo and Juliet, Mercutio makes jokes after a tense fight scene. Which literary term does this illustrate?
Explain how dramatic irony is used in the tomb scene where Romeo finds Juliet. Write one sentence using the term 'dramatic irony' correctly.
guidedPractice.answer: Dramatic irony is used because the audience knows Juliet has taken a sleeping potion and is not truly dead, but Romeo does not know this and believes she is dead, leading him to take his own life.

reteachModules.trigger: The student's open response on Q6 lacks key requirements for the Unit 3 Assignment 2 creative writing task.
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: The student thinks the assignment is simply to write any ending, and does not remember the exact constraints: only Act 5 may be rewritten, Romeo and Juliet and one extra character must appear, at least 5 dialogue lines are needed, one literary device must be used, the length must be 300–500 words, and 3 supporting questions must be answered.

miniLesson.explain: In this assignment you rewrite only Act 5 of Romeo and Juliet. You may choose a happy ending, an alternative tragedy, or a twist ending. Your rewrite must include Romeo, Juliet, and at least one extra character. You must have at least 5 lines of dialogue and use at least one literary device: symbolism, dramatic irony, or foreshadowing. The whole rewrite must be 300–500 words. After the rewrite, you must answer 3 supporting questions about theme, moral lesson, or character behaviour, using 2–3 sentences each. Submit your assignment as a single file to Dropbox; extensions are not allowed without serious circumstances.
miniLesson.example: For a happy ending, Friar Laurence's message reaches Romeo in time. He arrives at the tomb just as Juliet wakes. They embrace, and Romeo tells the Prince that the feud must end. The rewrite includes Romeo, Juliet, Friar Laurence, and 8 lines of dialogue. It uses dramatic irony: the audience knows Juliet's 'death' is fake, but Romeo does not. The word count is 450. After the rewrite, the student answers 3 questions: one about how the theme changes, one about the moral lesson, and one about Friar Laurence's decisions, each in 2–3 sentences.
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: 5-5-1-1-3: Act 5, 5+ dialogue lines, 1 extra character, 1 literary device, 3 supporting questions, and 300–500 words.

guidedPractice.prompt: Which of the following is NOT allowed in this assignment? A) Rewriting only Act 5, B) Changing Acts 1–4 to create a new backstory, C) Writing a twist ending, D) Including one extra character, E) Using dramatic irony.
guidedPractice.answer: B. You must rewrite only Act 5; the first four acts stay unchanged.

guidedPractice.prompt: Fill in the blanks: Your rewrite must be ____ to ____ words, contain at least ____ lines of dialogue, and use one literary device such as ____, ____, or ____. After the rewrite, you must answer ____ supporting questions, using ____ sentences each.
guidedPractice.answer: 300 to 500 words, 5 lines, symbolism/dramatic irony/foreshadowing, 3 supporting questions, 2–3 sentences each.

guidedPractice.prompt: A classmate's draft is 250 words, includes Romeo, Juliet, and the Nurse, has 4 lines of dialogue, uses no literary device, and does not include the supporting questions. List every missing requirement and identify which requirement is already met.
guidedPractice.answer: Missing: length too short (must be 300–500 words), dialogue too few (need at least 5 lines, draft has 4), no literary device (need symbolism, dramatic irony, or foreshadowing), no 3 supporting questions of 2–3 sentences each. Already met: extra character requirement (Nurse).

The fake death plan is attempted
Romeo and Juliet both die

questions.stem: Explain the cause-and-effect chain in the plot of Romeo and Juliet from the secret marriage to the final double suicide. Include the street brawl, Mercutio's death, and Romeo's exile. Write 2–4 sentences.
questions.rubric: Student correctly sequences the events: secret marriage leads to street brawls, Mercutio's death leads to Romeo's exile, the failed fake death plan leads to the double suicide. Response shows cause-and-effect links between events, not just a list.

retestCards.passRule: Both questions must be answered correctly. For the open-ended question, the response must reflect accurate sequencing and cause-and-effect reasoning as described in the rubric.

questions.stem: In a movie about two rival gangs, a boy and a girl fall in love, but a gang war leads to the boy's brother being killed, the girl's family forcing her to leave, and ultimately both run away and accidentally die. Which theme from Romeo and Juliet is most similar?
options: Love is more powerful than hate.
Gang violence is entertaining.
Inter-group hatred destroys love and causes tragedy.
Running away solves problems.

questions.stem: Explain why Romeo and Juliet is not just a teenage love story. Use at least two specific events from the play to support your answer.
questions.rubric: Response must identify that the play also explores the destructive power of family hatred, and must cite at least two plot events (e.g., street brawls, Mercutio's death, Romeo's exile, failed fake-death plan, double suicide) showing that the tragedy is caused by the Capulet-Montague feud, not simply by young love.

retestCards.passRule: Answer Q1 correctly AND provide a Q2 response that mentions the feud's destructive role and includes at least two specific plot events from the play.

questions.stem: When Juliet appears to be dead, the audience knows she took a sleeping potion, but Romeo does not. What literary device does this situation create?
options: A) Monologue
B) Soliloquy
C) Comic relief
D) Dramatic irony

questions.stem: Explain the difference between a soliloquy and an aside. In your answer, give one example of each from Romeo and Juliet.
questions.rubric: Student correctly defines soliloquy as a long speech by a character alone on stage that reveals inner thoughts, and an aside as a brief remark heard only by the audience. Student provides a relevant example of each from Romeo and Juliet, such as Romeo's soliloquy in the balcony scene or Juliet's aside during the party. Accept reasonable variations.

retestCards.passRule: To pass, the student must select the correct option on the multiple-choice question (Dramatic irony) and provide an open-ended response that accurately defines soliloquy and aside, with appropriate examples from Romeo and Juliet.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a required element for the Act 5 rewrite assignment?
options: A new character not in the original play
At least 5 lines of dialogue
A monologue by Juliet
Exactly 400 words

questions.stem: A peer's draft does not meet the assignment. The draft is 280 words, includes Romeo, Juliet, and the Nurse, has 6 lines of dialogue, uses foreshadowing, but does not include the supporting questions. Identify all the missing requirements and state which requirement is already met.
questions.rubric: Must identify that the draft is too short (must be 300–500 words) and missing the 3 supporting questions (each 2–3 sentences). Must also state that at least one requirement is already met (e.g., extra character, dialogue, or literary device).

retestCards.passRule: Question 1 must have the correct answer (option B). For question 2, the response must correctly identify at least two missing requirements (one of which must be the supporting questions or word count) and state at least one already-met requirement.

teacherEscalation.condition: student fails the same retest twice or scores in the lowest tier on two consecutive lesson diagnostics
teacherEscalation.message: 该学生需要人工短辅导；问题不是单题错误，而是核心概念系统没有建立。

dashboardFormat.objective: Romeo and Juliet is a tragedy by William Shakespeare, first performed in 1597, set in Verona, Italy.；The play centers on the feud between the Capulet and Montague families.；Plot: secret marriage, street brawls, Mercutio's death, Romeo's exile, failed fake death plan, double suicide.

learningGoals.statement: Understand the background, plot, and central theme of Romeo and Juliet.
Identify and explain key Shakespearean dramatic terms.
Recall and interpret the requirements for the Unit 3 Assignment 2 creative writing task.

courseOpsItems.title: Unit 3 Assignment 2 – Rewrite Act 5 Ending
courseOpsItems.studentAction: Write a 300-500 word adaptation of the Act 5 ending, keeping consistency with the first four acts. Choose one of three ending types: happy, alternative tragedy, or unexpected twist. Include Romeo, Juliet, and at least one additional character, with at least 5 lines of standard quoted dialogue. Integrate at least one literary device: symbolism, dramatic irony, or foreshadowing. Answer 3 supporting questions (each 2-3 complete sentences) about theme, moral lesson, and character behavior.
courseOpsItems.sourceEvidence: Students only need to rewrite the Act 5 ending of Romeo and Juliet... must include Romeo, Juliet, and at least one extra character, with no less than 5 lines of standard quoted dialogue... 300 to 500 words... 3 supporting questions about core theme, moral lesson, and character behavior support.

courseOpsItems.title: Submission Requirement: Single File to Dropbox, No Extensions
courseOpsItems.studentAction: Submit the completed assignment as a single file to the designated Dropbox folder. Do not request extensions unless there are serious special circumstances.
courseOpsItems.sourceEvidence: The completed assignment must be submitted as a single file to the designated Dropbox folder, no extensions are approved without serious special circumstances.

courseOpsItems.title: Wrap Up Remaining Unit 3 Tasks and KWS Worksheet
courseOpsItems.studentAction: Use the post-class work period to finish remaining Unit 3 tasks, check homework answer keys, and fill in the KWS worksheet as required.
courseOpsItems.sourceEvidence: Students can use the post-class work period to wrap up remaining Unit 3 tasks, check homework answer keys, and fill in the KWS worksheet as required.

cards.question: Who wrote Romeo and Juliet and when was it first performed?
options: William Shakespeare, 1597
Christopher Marlowe, 1595
William Shakespeare, 1601
Ben Jonson, 1597
cards.diagnosis: Check if student knows who wrote the play and when it was first performed.
misconceptions: ✓ Correct! Shakespeare wrote this tragedy early in his career, and it was first performed in 1597.
Not quite. The author is William Shakespeare; Marlowe was a different playwright of the same period.
Shakespeare wrote it earlier – the first performance was in 1597, not 1601.
Ben Jonson wrote other plays, but Romeo and Juliet is definitely by William Shakespeare.
cards.successCriteria: Student can recall the author, genre, and first performance date of Romeo and Juliet.
cards.ossdExpectation: Read and demonstrate understanding of a variety of texts for different purposes.
cards.alignmentNote: This question directly assesses comprehension of the literary text's background.
cards.commonMisconception: Students may confuse the author with another Elizabethan playwright or the premier date with a later performance.

cards.question: What is the central conflict in Romeo and Juliet?
options: A war between the cities of Verona and Mantua
A long-standing feud between the Capulet and Montague families
Romeo's argument with his father about marriage
A rivalry between two schools in Verona
cards.diagnosis: Check if student understands what drives the story's conflict.
misconceptions: The play is not about a war between cities; it's about a personal feud inside Verona.
✓ Yes! The entire story is built on the hatred between the two noble families.
Romeo's father is not a major source of conflict; the family feud is the driving force.
There are no schools involved; it's a deadly family rivalry.
cards.successCriteria: Student correctly identifies the central feud as the Capulet-Montague family conflict.
cards.ossdExpectation: Read and demonstrate understanding of a variety of texts for different purposes.
cards.alignmentNote: Asking about core conflict checks basic comprehension of the play's framework.
cards.commonMisconception: Students may think the conflict is between individual characters (e.g., Romeo vs. Tybalt) rather than families.

cards.question: Which of the following is a key event from the plot of Romeo and Juliet?
options: Romeo and Juliet hold a public wedding ceremony
Mercutio is killed by Tybalt, which leads to Romeo's exile
Juliet's plan to fake her death succeeds without any problems
Romeo kills Prince Escalus in a fight
cards.diagnosis: Check if student knows the key turning point in the plot.
misconceptions: They actually marry in secret, not in public.
✓ Right! Mercutio's death is the turning point that sets Romeo's banishment in motion.
The plan goes wrong because Romeo does not receive the message that she is only asleep.
Romeo kills Tybalt, not the Prince. Prince Escalus is the ruler of Verona.
cards.successCriteria: Student can identify a major plot event from a list of possibilities.
cards.ossdExpectation: Read and demonstrate understanding of a variety of texts for different purposes.
cards.alignmentNote: This question tests whether the student followed the sequence of events in the tragedy.
cards.commonMisconception: Students often forget the order of deaths or the exile, confusing it with other events.

cards.question: According to the lesson, what is the main theme of Romeo and Juliet?
options: Young love always overcomes every obstacle
Meaningless inter-group hatred can lead to irreversible tragedy
If you believe in fate, everything will end happily
Friendship is more important than romantic love
cards.diagnosis: Check if student can articulate the lesson's deeper message about hatred.
misconceptions: The play actually shows how love is destroyed by hatred, not how it conquers all.
✓ Exactly! The lesson emphasized that Shakespeare uses the lovers' deaths to show the terrible cost of the family feud.
Fate does not bring happiness here – the 'star-crossed' lovers die.
While friendship is present (Mercutio, Nurse), the central theme is about hatred and its consequences.
cards.successCriteria: Student can go beyond the love story and explain the destructive cost of inter-group hatred as the central theme.
cards.ossdExpectation: Read and demonstrate understanding of a variety of texts for different purposes.
cards.alignmentNote: Asking about theme moves from comprehension to interpretation, fulfilling the 'demonstrate understanding' portion of B1.
cards.commonMisconception: Students often reduce the play to a teenage romance and miss the broader social commentary.

cards.question: Which of the following is an example of dramatic irony?
options: Romeo speaks about his feelings while alone on stage
The audience knows Juliet is just asleep, but Romeo believes she is dead
The Nurse makes a joke after a serious scene
Friar Laurence delivers a speech about the power of plants
cards.diagnosis: Check if student knows what dramatic irony means in a dramatic context.
misconceptions: That is a soliloquy – a character thinking aloud when alone.
✓ Correct! Dramatic irony occurs when the audience knows something important that a character does not.
That is comic relief – a humorous moment to lighten the mood.
That is a monologue – a long speech by one character to others on stage.
cards.successCriteria: Student can match the definition of dramatic irony to an example.
cards.ossdExpectation: Read and demonstrate understanding of a variety of texts for different purposes.
cards.alignmentNote: Identifying literary devices is part of demonstrating understanding of texts under B1.
cards.commonMisconception: Students often confuse soliloquy, aside, and dramatic irony because they all involve audience knowledge.

cards.question: List at least three key requirements for the Unit 3 Assignment 2 (rewriting the ending of Romeo and Juliet).
cards.diagnosis: Check if student knows what is expected in the assignment before beginning to write.
cards.successCriteria: Student can recall and list at least three specific requirements of the creative writing assignment.
cards.ossdExpectation: Write in a variety of forms for different purposes and audiences.
cards.alignmentNote: This question directly assesses the student's readiness to produce a written piece following specific genre and task instructions, which aligns with C1.
cards.commonMisconception: Students often miss one or two requirements (e.g., forget the minimum number of lines or the need for an extra character) and then lose marks.
